extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners (attorneys/agents before the USPTO), USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline staff, and legal professionals involved in practitioner discipline
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements governing a patent practitioner’s duty of candor/disclosure to the USPTO and the disciplinary/resolution process (settlement, sanctions, publication, and notice) under USPTO rules and MPEP guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of candor and good faith (37 C.F.R. § 1.56)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each individual associated with the filing and prosecution of a patent application has a duty of candor and good faith in dealing with the Office, including a duty to disclose to the Office all information known to that individual to be material to patentability. The duty to disclose information exists with respect to each pending claim until the claim is cancelled or withdrawn from consideration, or the application becomes abandoned. 37 C.F.R. § 1.56(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to every person involved in prosecution; failure to disclose material information (e.g., related litigation or adverse decisions) can constitute misconduct. The duty persists claim-by-claim until cancellation/withdrawal/abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of litigation-related material information (MPEP § 2001.06(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the subject matter for which a patent is being sought is or has been involved in litigation, the existence of such litigation and any other material information arising therefrom must be brought to the attention of the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patent application or related subject matter has been part of litigation, practitioners must inform the Office of both the pendency of that litigation and material information arising from it (for example, district court decisions affecting enforceability). Non-disclosure of such litigation is an example of an actionable omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality standard tied to pending claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty to disclose information known to be material to patentability is tied to each pending claim and lasts until the claim is cancelled, withdrawn from consideration, or the application becomes abandoned (37 C.F.R. § 1.56(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must evaluate materiality with respect to the status of each claim. Information that affects patentability of any pending claim must be disclosed while that claim remains under consideration; abandoning or cancelling claims changes disclosure obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary violation: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice by not informing the Office of the pendency of, and final decision in, a federal district court case concerning the enforceability of a U.S. patent (as found in this case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose material litigation or adverse decisions to the USPTO may be charged under Disciplinary Rule 10.23(b)(5); such a charge can lead to public discipline even if deceptive intent is disputed. The Final Order here adjudicated such a violation based on stipulated facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for Proposed Settlement Agreements (37 C.F.R. § 11.26)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Proposed Settlement Agreement must set forth certain stipulated facts, legal conclusions, and sanctions to resolve disciplinary complaints and must satisfy the requirements of 37 C.F.R. § 11.26; it is submitted to the USPTO Director (or designate) for approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A properly framed settlement will resolve all disciplinary action arising from the stipulated facts; the Final Order should set forth the stipulated facts, legal conclusions, and the agreed discipline. Settlement is subject to Director approval and statutory/regulatory requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional basis for USPTO disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director has jurisdiction over practitioner disciplinary matters pursuant to the provisions of 35 U.S.C. §§ 2 and 32 and 37 C.F.R. § 11.26.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary proceedings, settlement approval, and issuance of Final Orders rely on these statutory and regulatory jurisdictional provisions; practitioners and counsel should be aware that USPTO authority to discipline flows from these sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions, publication, and notification procedures (37 C.F.R. § 11.59 and related provisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions available and procedures include public reprimand, publication of the Final Order, publication of a Notice in the Official Gazette describing the reprimand and the basis for it, and giving notice of the public discipline and reasons to disciplinary enforcement agencies in the State where the practitioner is admitted, to courts where the practitioner is known to be admitted, and to the public (in accordance with 37 C.F.R. § 11.59).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order exemplifies the form of Official Gazette notice (practitioner name, registration number, statement of violation, and mention of mitigating facts). The OED Director handles publication and notices; parties typically bear their own costs unless otherwise ordered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of mitigating factors (absence of deceptive intent)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner's representation that he did not act with deceptive intent (e.g., did not intend to deceive the Office by failing to disclose litigation or decisions) is a disclosed mitigating factor considered in resolution and sanctioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admissions about intent (or lack thereof) are relevant to sanction selection; absence of deceptive intent may lead to lesser sanctions (e.g., reprimand rather than suspension or disbarment), but does not preclude discipline for the underlying omission.
